findings.title: The initiative's core goal has no mechanism: nothing positions the workflow after adoption
findings.description: The Overview (line 20), Design Goals (line 40), Navigation (line 104) and Adoption flow step 6 all promise `cf next` "points at the first new slice" after adoption, with "the normal phases continue with `cf build` as everywhere else". The architecture never says who registers the derived artifacts or advances workflow state. `WorkflowNavigator` (`packages/core/src/introspection/WorkflowNavigator.ts`) derives everything from `ResolvedProject` config: `parseSlicePlanSafe()` returns `null` when `project.fileSlicePlan` is unset, `deriveSliceStatus()` needs `project.fileSlice`, and `detectFirstRunContext()` branches on `project.developmentPhase`. `cf init` (`buildProjectCreationDefaults` in `packages/core/src/project-defaults.ts`) sets `developmentPhase: 'Phase 0: Concept'` and leaves `fileArch`, `fileSlicePlan` and `fileSlice` empty. The adoption flow's step 5 says only "the agent writes the derived architecture and the existing-state slice plan" — writing markdown files. With no `cf set arch` / `cf set plan` / `cf set slice` / `cf set phase` step anywhere in the architecture, a freshly adopted project has a concept doc, so `detectFirstRunContext()` returns "Concept document exists. Advance to Phase 1 (Initiative Plan)" (`WorkflowNavigator.ts:669`) and the retroactive/new slice entries are invisible. Neither the responsibility table (rows c/d/g) nor slice 263/271 claims this registration. This is the load-bearing omission: the stated goal is unachievable as written.

findings.title: The `fileComprehension` handoff cannot be delivered by the proposed primitive
findings.description: Step 4 and the amended guide-prompt contract (line 136) say the prompt is "delivered by the slice 271 primitive with the comprehension path filled in", and that "Slice 271's design settles how the profile's variables are delivered". This is the *only* cf↔squadron contact point left (principle, line 50), and it is deferred. In the actual stack, `fileComprehension` is not a prompt placeholder: it is a field on `EnhancedContextData` that `ContextIntegrator.mapProjectToEnhancedContext()` sets and `SectionBuilder.buildProjectInfoSection()` renders as a `Comprehension: ...` line during `cf build`, with `applyProfileFiltering()` gating it on the `brownfield-adoption` context profile. Slice 268 deletes adoption from `cf build`, so that entire path disappears. The guide's current Brownfield Adoption prompt (`project-documents/ai-project-guide/project-guides/prompt.ai-project.system.md:444-476`) contains no `{fileComprehension}` token at all, and `cf prompt get` (`packages/cli/src/commands/prompt.ts`) substitutes from a fixed seven-variable map with no comprehension, concept, arch or slice-plan variable. Combined with the "Guide owns content, cf owns logic / cf hard-codes none of their wording" principle (line 53), cf cannot inject the path into prompt text without either editing guide wording or inventing a cf-owned appended fragment — a mechanism the architecture does not describe. An architecture that makes its single cross-repo handoff undefined at the design stage is not implementable.

findings.title: The retroactive marker is a user-editable review-gate bypass, and the architecture claims the loophole is closed
findings.description: The Baseline artifacts section asserts "A retroactive entry with a slice design or task file is a checker error. Real new work always produces those files, so the marker can't be used to bypass the gate." The shipped implementation contradicts this. The marker is a backticked prose token in a checklist line (`guide.ai-project.brownfield-adoption.md`: `1. [x] **(100) Existing System** \`retroactive\` — ...`), so any agent or human can add it to a new slice. `WorkflowNavigator.deriveSliceStatus()` returns `STATUS.Complete` for a checked retroactive entry with the comment "no gate is evaluated", and `reviewGate.evaluateEntryGate()` returns `status: 'skipped'` at every slice-scoped boundary. `ruleRetroactiveEntries()` (`packages/core/src/introspection/retroactiveRules.ts`) only errors when a design/task file *already exists* — an agent that marks a new slice retroactive and simply writes no design gets a silent pass through the review gate. This is functionally the PM-only `review: none` exemption that 240 and guide v0.17.4 reserve for the PM, but reachable by editing a checkbox line. It also violates the project convention "NEVER use user-accessible labels as logical structure. They are fragile": a label in prose is being used to control gating, checker and pipeline behavior (squadron row (d) reads slice status). The architecture should specify a non-user-authored provenance check or an explicit PM decision for the marker, not assert the loophole is closed by a post-hoc checker.

findings.title: Detection precedence contradicts "derived from the files", and `cf next` cannot actually consume the report
findings.description: "One detection, many consumers" says the outcome is "decided once, in core ... exposed as a read-only report (CLI and MCP) that `sq onboard`, `cf init` and `cf next` consume. Nothing persists the outcome: it is derived from the files every time." Three problems. (1) The Detection section (lines 75-79) puts **Opted out** first ("It is greenfield") ahead of **Already planned**, so a stored config value outranks the files even for a repo holding an architecture and slice plan — directly contradicting the amendment's "the files say whether a project is planned, and only an opt-out is stored". For such a repo detection says greenfield while the navigator follows the artifacts, so the two surfaces disagree. (2) `WorkflowNavigator.getNext(project)` takes a `ResolvedProject` built from registered config, not a detection report; after slice 270 removes `routeAdoption`/`adoptionNavigation.ts`, there is no described input by which the "one line for an unadopted brownfield repo" (line 104) is computed. (3) `cf init` is a mutating command (`packages/cli/src/commands/init.ts` runs `git init`, `store.create`, guide/command/IDE install) yet is named a consumer of a read-only report; the architecture never says whether the "print one line" call happens before or after those writes, or on which `cf init` paths (`--lite`, MCP `project_create`). The wiring decisions that the whole principle depends on are absent.

findings.title: No error handling or recovery for a failed or partial adoption
findings.description: The amendment removes the state machine with "the files say whether a project is planned", and "Additive and reversible" (line 52) claims reversibility. But a `sq onboard` run that fails after writing the concept, after the graph build errors, or after the agent writes only the architecture leaves artifacts that make the project "Already planned" (Detection step 2), so step 2 of the adoption flow says "adoption doesn't apply" and there is no way back in — the opt-out only forces greenfield, and no un-adopt/rollback path exists. The pre-amendment design's "a re-run resumes from whatever artifacts exist" (line 136, original contract) was removed with no replacement. Also unaddressed: a comprehension doc that is stale or absent when the prompt is delivered; a graph build that fails or is declined at the PM ask (step 3); conflicts between squadron's written concept and the guide prompt's draft (two writers are still named in the Concept row, line 125, while step 5 says the agent drafts it). "It asks the PM once before a paid graph build" is the only failure-adjacent sentence in the whole flow. No component is assigned ownership of detecting, reporting, or unwinding a partial adoption.

findings.title: Guide release coupling and Dependencies describe a release that no longer applies, and a stale guide hard-stops the delivered prompt
findings.description: The "Guide release coupling" section announces in parentheses that the fail-fast rule "moves to the prompt-delivery primitive", then immediately restates the removed behavior: "If cf selects the brownfield profile and the installed guide lacks it, `cf build` fails with a named error." The Dependencies bullet (line 159) still says "cf releases that select the brownfield profile require at least **v0.22.2** (v0.22.2 fixed the squadron-path gate in the brownfield prompt)" — that fix concerns probe branching which the amendment says "goes away" — and claims "Still pending": the retroactive-marker rule (shipped in guide v0.22.3, `guide.ai-project.brownfield-adoption.md` "Retroactive Slices") and the docs-map naming entry (shipped in v0.22.6, `file-naming-conventions.md:518`, and implemented in `packages/core/src/docs-map/docsMapFile.ts`). The installed guide is v0.22.7; `MIN_GUIDE_VERSION` is `'0.22.6'` (`packages/core/src/guides/guideMinimum.ts`), and slice 272 plans to "Raise MIN_GUIDE_VERSION to the guide release that carries that" with no such release named. Concretely, the guide's current Brownfield Adoption prompt still says "If the section is missing, stop and say: 'The Adoption Facts section is missing; cf build should always supply it'" and "Re-run `cf build`", so the slice-271 primitive delivers a prompt that hard-stops on an input cf deliberately no longer produces. Slice 268's own Risk note acknowledges this, but `checkGuideMinimum()` is only a warning (260 slice design D8 explicitly rejected failing the build), so a stale guide silently produces a broken adoption run. The architecture must name the required guide version, order it before 271, and make the primitive fail fast when the delivered prompt is incompatible.

findings.title: The cross-repo contract that squadron must build against is not specified
findings.description: The report is "exposed as one CLI command and one MCP tool returning JSON (slice 271)" and is "the contract between cf and squadron ... which squadron calls" (line 135). No command name, no JSON schema, no field types for "source volume (a floor), history, docs, ADRs, CI and rule files", no outcome vocabulary beyond the three prose labels, no error/exit-code semantics, and no statement of whether `sq onboard` calls the CLI or the MCP tool. Slice 271's success criteria push all of this to slice design ("The slice design settles command names") — but this is the extension point on which the entire adoption path depends, and adoption is parked until squadron builds against it. Likewise the opt-out's config key, who writes it (`cf config set`? squadron? an MCP tool?), and whether squadron can read it are never defined, even though "Opted out" is detection step 1. No versioning or compatibility rule is given for the report, so a field rename in cf silently breaks an external consumer. A cross-repo contract deferred to a slice design is not an extension point; it is an unbuilt interface.

findings.title: Detection failure modes and per-command cost are unwired
findings.description: "Brownfield thresholds" says "Signals and thresholds are set in slice design; the override is the safety valve", with no error strategy for the read-only report itself. The existing core implementation that 271 must expose has two hard failure modes the architecture never mentions: `measureSourceVolume()` (`packages/core/src/detection/sourceVolume.ts`) throws `AdoptionError` after `MAX_WALK_ENTRIES = 20_000` directory entries without reaching `BROWNFIELD_MIN_SOURCE_LINES = 2000` — a large asset-heavy or vendored repo makes detection *fail*, not report a fact — and `readHistory()` (`history.ts`) spawns `git rev-list` with a 5-second timeout on every call. Since `cf next` is named a consumer of the report and runs constantly, every navigation call on an unadopted brownfield repo pays an async tree walk plus a worst-case 5s git subprocess, with no caching, no validated latency assumption, and no described behavior when either fails (warning? error? no one-line guidance?). The CLI/MCP "writes nothing" guarantee also isn't reconciled with `readHistory`'s subprocess or with `cf init`'s existing habit of swallowing setup failures as `warn(...)`. Project conventions require explicit errors rather than silent fallbacks; the architecture supplies neither.

findings.title: The document is two contradictory architectures layered together; un-amended sections state shipped-and-reversed facts as current
findings.description: The amendment says "the sections below are rewritten to match", but they are not. "Squadron contract stability (superseded)" (line 135) and "Guide prompt contract" (line 136) preserve the entire original design "for history" while ending with present-tense claims — "CF tests check the field names as a cross-repo contract, and CF treats an unknown version or unreadable output as 'squadron unavailable'" — behavior slice 271 deletes (`packages/core/tests/detection/squadronProbe.contract.test.ts` is exactly that test). "Anticipated Slices" (lines 145-153) presents the reversed plan — "persisted adoption state", "`cf build` selecting the `brownfield-adoption` profile", "reading the probe", "adoption steps while in progress" — as "In expected order" with no superseded marker on the bullets. "Current State" (lines 57-63) is un-amended and now false: it says three "hand-written copies" of the onboard recipe "already drift", but slice 260 shipped `packages/core/src/onboarding/onboardRecipe.ts` rendered to all three surfaces with a drift test; it says `/setup-ci` "fires only when `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is absent", but `recognizeCi` now covers eight signatures; it says the capability probe "does not exist yet" while cf shipped `squadronProbe.ts` and is deleting it. The responsibility table still lists squadron 361/362/363/364/366/400/440 rows and "It is frozen until the handoff contract settles". A reader cannot tell which design is authoritative.

findings.title: Overweight architecture for a five-slice deletion-and-two-primitives rework
findings.description: The actual deliverable (slices 268–272) is mostly deletion: remove adoption from `cf build`/`context_build`/`template_preview`, collapse a four-value state to an opt-out, delete `adoptionNavigation.ts` and the probe integration, add one read-only JSON report and one prompt delivery, update docs. 273–274 are parked. Yet the architecture carries two full obsolete contracts (~1,000 words of probe field schemas and Adoption Facts/`/understand` branching at lines 135-136), a superseded seven-bullet slice plan, a 12-row cross-repo responsibility table including squadron 400/440/361/363/364/366, a guide-version changelog in Dependencies, and a "Current State" inventory of code that no longer exists. Cut: the entire "for history" probe and guide-prompt contracts (move to a `decisions` or archive note), the shipped-and-reversed "Anticipated Slices" list (the slice plan at `260-slices.brownfield-adoption.md` already records it), the stale Current State bullets, the guide release-by-release dependency prose, and the squadron initiative rows cf neither knows nor tests ("Squadron decides its own surfaces, graph freshness and plugin requirements"). What should remain is short and precise: the detection report schema and outcome precedence, the opt-out key, the prompt-delivery contract (including how the comprehension path reaches the agent), the retroactive-marker contract with its gate semantics, and the post-adoption state-registration step. As written, the most load-bearing decisions are the ones absent, while the largest sections document decisions that were reversed.
